item.title: Trump signs executive order waiving new Russia sanctions, tariffs
item.description: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia’s energy revenues after signing them into law last month. The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — allowed Trump the authority to impose duties up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. “As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” the executive order said. The law targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. Trump’s reversal on the Russia sanctions comes in after a controversial deal he struck with Putin that would allow Russia diesel exports in exchange for US sanctions relief. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since the deal, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling it a “weak decision” and Ukrainian forces resuming attacks on Russian oil refineries. Nigeria’s revolving door of arrest, release and relapse According to Ikpechukwu, drug use does not occur in isolation. For many young people, it intersects with unemployment, economic pressure, trauma, peer influence, family stress and social exclusion. In his presentation, Ikpechukwu’s argument brought the intersection of public health and justice into focus. A young person’s encounter with the justice system, he showed, can become either a revolving door of arrest, release and repeat offending or a turning point towards assessment, treatment and recovery. He challenged the country to rethink its response to youth drug addiction and the intersection between substance use disorders and the criminal justice system. In his presentation, Ikpechukwu posed a question that went to the heart of the debate: “Which pathway better protects the young person, the family and society?” His argument was not that drug-related offences should be excused or that addiction should become a blanket defence against criminal responsibility. The scale of the challenge was underscored by the UNIDOC’s national drug-use survey, conducted in 2018 and published in 2019. The survey estimated that 14.3 million Nigerians aged 15 to 64 had used drugs in the previous year. item.title: DSS, military, police arrest 5 over NYSC members kidnap
item.description: …As 3 others escape with gunshot injuries By Soni Daniel Operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS), the military and police have arrested five suspected members of a criminal gang allegedly responsible for the abduction of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members in Imo State on Nigeria’s 66th Independence Day. Five other suspected members of the gang, however, escaped with gunshot injuries prompting a massive manhunt for them. The suspects were apprehended during a series of intelligence-led operations conducted at different locations in Rivers and Abia States. However, in the course of the operation, three other suspects escaped with varying degrees of injury. Security sources disclosed that the operations were carried out between October 10 and 14 in Port Harcourt, Rivers State and Aba South LGA. Abia State. Recall that 20 NYSC members were abducted by armed men along Owerri–Onitsha Expressway in Imo State on October 1, 2026, as they travelled to their assigned orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states. The victims were subsequently rescued on October 7, 2026, during a joint security operation at Amakohia Ubi Village. The string of operations mark a significant breakthrough in efforts to track down the perpetrators, dismantle the criminal network allegedly responsible for the abduction and bring those involved to justice. A security source described the development as a major relief, noting that security agencies had sustained a wide-ranging manhunt for the abductors. “This is a huge sigh of relief. Security agencies have been on a manhunt for the abductors, and we are elated that they have been captured. We strongly believe they will be charged to Court by DSS and the corps members will get justice,” the source said. item.title: NFF Normalisation Committee: FIFA keeps Nigeria waiting
item.description: The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) is still awaiting clarification from FIFA following Thursday’s FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, Switzerland, amid expectations that the country’s football leadership crisis would be on the front burner. The FIFA Council held its 37th meeting on October 15, 2026, with discussions covering football development funding, governance reforms and disciplinary procedures. However, FIFA’s published statement on the meeting did not confirm whether the Council approved the proposed Normalisation Committee for Nigeria. The absence of a public announcement does not necessarily mean Nigeria’s situation was not discussed behind closed doors. Among the key developments, FIFA announced plans to increase football development investment to US$6.35 billion for the 2027–2030 cycle, covering its 211 member associations, confederations and other stakeholders. The proposed framework could allow individual member associations to receive allocations of up to US$25 million, subject to applicable requirements and approval procedures. The Council also agreed to establish a working group to examine FIFA’s governance framework and directed relevant committees to review disciplinary procedures. The meeting attracted particular interest in Nigeria following the August resignations of former NFF President Ibrahim Gusau, General Secretary Mohammed Sanusi and members of the federation’s executive board. A joint FIFA and Confederation of African Football (CAF) delegation subsequently visited Nigeria in September to consult stakeholders and examine possible solutions to the crisis. One option reportedly under consideration is a Normalisation Committee to manage the federation temporarily, implement reforms and organise elections. Earlier reports indicated that the matter could be considered under the FIFA Council’s miscellaneous agenda. On Thursday October 15, Nigerian football stakeholders waited in vain for official clarification on whether FIFA will constitute a Normalisation Committee and issue a timetable for restoring elected leadership. item.title: 2027: ‘I won’t restore petrol subsidy’ — YPP candidate Agada
item.description: The presidential candidate of the Young Progressives Party (YPP), Peter Agada, has ruled out restoring petrol subsidy if elected president in the 2027 general elections, saying he would retain the policy introduced by President Bola Tinubu. Agada made this known on Friday during an interview on Channels Television’s Politics Today , where he outlined his approach to addressing Nigeria’s revenue and expenditure challenges. Tinubu announced the removal of petrol subsidy during his inauguration on May 29, 2023, a decision that led to higher petrol prices and increased the cost of goods and services. While some presidential hopefuls, including African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate Atiku Abubakar, have advocated restoring the subsidy to reduce fuel costs and ease economic hardship, Agada said his administration would maintain its removal. “I will stick to the gun with the present administration. We will remove subsidy the way they have done,” he said. The YPP candidate argued that Nigeria’s economic challenges were not solely a consequence of subsidy removal but were also linked to how the country manages oil revenues and the expenses incurred in producing crude oil. Citing remarks by the Minister of State for Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, Agada questioned how much revenue the Federal Government actually retains from crude oil production after royalties and other deductions. He argued that the amount left for the government was insufficient to meet the country’s needs, despite its oil production capacity. Agada said his administration would scrutinise the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) system to identify waste and improve government revenue. “We want to interrogate that system because we think that the wastage and majority of the challenges Nigeria is facing in terms of lower revenue is coming from that whole regime or that system that Nigeria practices,” he said. He maintained that the system had been faulty from its inception and required reforms to address inefficiencies. Agada acknowledged that Nigeria faced both revenue and expenditure problems but said excessive or inefficient spending was the more pressing concern. He argued that improving public expenditure management and plugging leakages would be central to addressing the country’s economic difficulties without reversing the petrol subsidy removal policy. Against the background of plans by political parties to set up situation rooms to collate results that have been announced by electoral officials at the polling units, the INEC has therefore warned media organisations not to publish privately collated election results. INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, gave the warning on Thursday September 24, 2026 while speaking at the 24th All Nigeria Editors Conference (ANEC 2026), organised by the Nigerian Guild of Editors in Enugu. He said the media should resist the temptation to publish election results generated by political actors or other private organisations before the commission makes official declarations. The INEC chairman repeated the warning on Tuesday, October 6, 2026 in Abuja at a national stakeholders’ meeting convened to mark 100 days to the 2027 general election arguing that under the Electoral Act, the authority to declare results rests exclusively with the commission. The commission’s warning has therefore provoked reactions from Nigerians who expect their votes to count during the election and look forward to the commission to conduct credible, transparent and fair general elections. Meeting this expectation therefore requires the establishment of transparent processes through which they can independently examine electoral records. In a letter dated October 12, 2026 addressed to the INEC chairman, the former president of the Nigerian Bar Association, NBA, Dr Olisa Agbakoba, SAN, said the commission’s exclusive authority to declare election results formally should not be interpreted as a restriction on the public’s right to report results already announced at polling units or contained in authentic electoral records. Dr Agbakoba drew a distinction between declaration of final election results by INEC and announcement of preliminary results by media organisations. According to him, “While INEC retains its exclusive statutory responsibility for the formal declaration of results, nothing in that responsibility should be understood as prohibiting citizens or the media from reporting results that have been publicly announced at polling units or from publishing information contained in authentic INEC electoral records (Forms EC8A – EC8E), provided that such reporting is accurate and does not misrepresent the official records. “Where polling-unit result sheets are uploaded and made accessible through IReV, citizens, journalists, political parties and observers can view those records, assess them and communicate their contents accurately, while clearly identifying the source and status of the information”. He argued that Section 25 of the Electoral Act, 2026, which governs the relevant functions of electoral officers, must be read alongside other applicable provisions of the Act and “Section 39(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, as amended, which guarantees the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to hold opinions and to receive and impart ideas and information without interference. This constitutional protection is central to the question of whether citizens and the media may communicate information about electoral results that are already publicly available”. Dr Agbakoba then cited the 1984 judgment delivered by Justice Candide Johnson of the High Court of Lagos State in a case between the Nigeria Union of Journalists and the Inspector General of Police where the court declared as unlawful and unconstitutional, the directive by Federal Electoral Commission, FEDECO, (now INEC) warning the media not to publish election results that had not been officially released by it. He therefore urged the Commission to understand the clear distinction between the formal declaration of results and the lawful publication or projection of electoral outcomes based on verifiable records and guarantee the citizens and the media the right to publish and analyse election results from authentic polling unit records ahead of the 2027 general elections. Dr Agbakoba also appeared on Arise News television programme, The Morning Show, last Wednesday to share his perspective on INEC’s warning against the media or the citizens publishing election results. During the programme, he was asked how the public can ensure accuracy of the results announced by the citizens which are already in the public domain and if he intended to take any consequential steps to defend his position. His response: “No, I don’t intend to take any consequential steps because already in 1984, Mr Justice Candide Johnson, in the case concerning NUJ and FEDECO, (now INEC), decided exactly what I’m saying; that journalists have a right to publish results. I think the confusion is that we confuse the declaration of results. That’s the only power that INEC has exclusively, to declare the results. But as you know, the electoral record in terms of voting goes from the polling unit to the ward, to the local government, to the state, to the national collation and to the final announcement. That is the process. If I’m standing at the polling unit and the presiding officer reads the results, I can broadcast it because he has read it. And I can tell you that political parties are going to set up AI processes whereby they’ll be able to pick results from the IReV, because the IReV is simply a compilation of all the results coming from the polling units. “So, this time I predict we’re going to see speed. item.title: Tell him he’s lying about tithe, by Fada Oluoma
item.description: You have worshipped in his church for 20 years since it’s beginning. You have faithfully paid tithes and other financial commitment to the church. Your finances have not magically or miraculously doubled, tripled or quadrupled. It is obvious that the progress you have made over the years is the result of your diligent work, same progress those in your kind of job or career have also witnessed including those that don’t tithe. Meanwhile this prophet/ pastor of yours screams almost every other Sunday that your tithe is your guaranteed way to financial prosperity. He uses himself as example of someone financially prosperous because he pays his tithe. You can see his mansion, exotic cars and and other evidence of a financially prosperous guy. Meanwhile he has no known business that brings him such money. Sometimes you wonder when your own breakthrough will come like his. Listen, this is not me against tithe. This is me trying one more time to help you say no to manipulation. You are one of the faithful believers whose financial sacrifices help us to carry out our pastoral duties, I appreciate you you for that, but we( the honest pastors) don’t want you doing that for the wrong reasons. Once more, tithing is one of the voluntary ways of financially supporting the church. It doesn’t have any superior supernatural blessing than other ways like offering, donations, levies, charity. If you are still paying tithe because you believe what some preachers tell you that it is your divine ticket to wealth, please stop, they are lying to you. Look around you and you will see that what I’m saying is true. That your pastor that boasts about financial prosperity because of the tithes he pays is lying. He is financially prosperous because of the tithes people pay to him, or because of the businesses he has established with them. After 40 years of paying tithe and you haven’t prospered like him, is your own coming as pension in your old age? I have people who give tithe in my small church every Sunday despite my position on tithe. I have told them this same truth multiple times and these people still come out. It simply tells me that telling the truth will never stop people from supporting the church. Back to you. Walk up to that your pastor and tell him to stop lying, tell him that you give your tithe as a commitment and not because it will make you wealthy. If God decides to use it to catapult you miraculously to wealth, thanks be to God. Just tell him to stop lying. Unless you believe him despite your condition. Sponsor of the bill, Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, representing Cross River South, had argued that criminal punishment could discourage people in distress from seeking help and push others towards more fatal attempts. I can’t imagine what would be in the mind of a Nigerian currently in a state of hopelessness and having thoughts of suicide as an easy way out. The approach Nigeria should adopt to ensure that vulnerable individuals trapped in the web of mental health challenges leading to suicidal thoughts do not carry it out, would be to have a strategic suicide prevention mechanism whereby a framework is developed to train suicide prevention professionals, advance more education and enlightenment to several communities including schools. Suicide prevention requires interventions that reduce risk, enable early help-seeking and ensure access to appropriate care. The question is not simply whether punishment exists, but whether the legal framework helps prevent deaths and supports people who need assistance. A law intended to discourage suicide may make it harder for the people most at risk to access the help they need. A person who survives a suicide attempt may be afraid of being judged, stigmatised or exposed publicly. item.title: Toyin Abraham debunks alleged leaked audio amid online backlash
item.description: By Tony-Okafor Favour Nollywood actress Toyin Abraham has broken her silence over the backlash trailing an alleged leaked audio conversation in which a TikTok fan was heard making disparaging remarks about fellow actress Funke Akindele. item.title: Westerhof diagnosed with colon cancer, critical
item.description: Former Super Eagles coach Clemens Westerhof has been diagnosed with colon cancer and is in critical condition at a hospital in Arnhem, his hometown in the Netherlands. His wife, Lilian, disclosed this to Saturday Editor Onochie Anibeze on Friday night, saying the 86-year-old was receiving treatment at Rijnstate Hospital. “The doctor just told us he has colon cancer and we are all devastated. He is in a critical condition and emotional, talking about our two daughters. He wants to live. We need help. We need prayers,” she said. Lilian said Westerhof was rushed to the hospital on Wednesday, adding that the cancer diagnosis was a new development in his health challenges. The Dutch tactician had been battling Alzheimer’s disease before the latest diagnosis. She expressed concern about the care Westerhof was receiving at the Arnhem hospital and said she hoped to move him to a better-equipped facility in Amsterdam or Germany. “They appear to have given up. I don’t understand,” she said. Westerhof, who turned 86 last May, is widely credited with helping to transform Nigerian football during his tenure as Super Eagles coach. He led Nigeria to qualify for its first-ever FIFA World Cup in 1994 and guided the team to victory at the Africa Cup of Nations in Tunisia the same year. Under his leadership, Nigeria also secured silver at the 1990 AFCON and bronze in 1992. The Super Eagles rose to fifth in the FIFA world rankings during his tenure, a landmark achievement for Nigerian and African football. The infrastructure is grossly inadequate. The facility is overcrowded. The pre-trial detention is prolonged. This has therefore raised questions about the country’s capacity to reform offenders while protecting the rights and dignity of persons in custody. Ageing infrastructure The physical condition of many correctional centres compounds the problem. Many facilities were constructed decades ago and are now operating beyond their original capacities. The House Committee on Reformatory Institutions recently warned that some facilities were built more than a century ago and have deteriorated significantly. An independent investigative panel established by the Federal Government to examine allegations of corruption, abuse of power and human rights violations within the correctional system also identified severe infrastructure deficits. The panel assessed 86 custodial facilities across 23 states and the Federal Capital Territory and raised concerns over security risks and infrastructural decay in several centres, including facilities in Delta, Edo, Sokoto and Kaduna states. But the cycle of interruption was not over. Then came 2026. In May 2026, the NRC again suspended the Warri–Itakpe service. This time, the corporation cited operational exigencies and technical advice from its engineers. It said the suspension was necessary to carry out critical operational assessments aimed at ensuring safety, reliability and improved service delivery. The service resumed again in January 2026 after another delay, with the NRC announcing scheduled operations between Ujevwu and Itakpe. But one of the most serious incidents came on June 8, 2026. A Warri–Itakpe train travelling from Itakpe derailed near Owa-Oyibu in Delta State. According to the NRC’s preliminary report, the train was carrying 482 people—442 passengers and 40 operational personnel. Four people died and 64 were injured The NRC said five coaches, one locomotive and a power car were affected, with three coaches and the power car overturning. The tragedy inevitably changed the conversation. It was no longer simply about delayed trains or inconvenient suspensions. It was about whether the railway could consistently deliver the most basic promise of public transportation: to take people to their destination safely. What caused the derailment? This question remains important because the answer is not yet final. The NRC’s August 2026 preliminary report said its internal investigation found a possible sudden bogie or wheel defect while the train was in motion. It also said the possible manner of brake application may have contributed to the severity of the incident. But the corporation stressed that these were working hypotheses, not definitive findings. An independent investigation by the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau is ongoing, and the final report remains pending. Significantly, the NRC said its investigators found no evidence of track vandalism at the June crash site. That distinction matters The corporation had previously attributed two incidents on the same service in November 2025 to track vandalism. The June 2026 incident, however, is being investigated on a different basis. The track has since been recovered and restored, according to the NRC. But the corporation says the locomotives are undergoing reconditioning and that service resumption will depend on detailed track and equipment safety audits. And Ujevwu waits This is where the statistics become human. For passengers, traders and residents around Ujevwu, every suspension has consequences. A railway station is rarely just a place where trains stop. It can support a small economy of food sellers, transport operators, traders, ticket agents and other informal businesses. Passengers who arrive at a station buy food, drinks and other necessities. Commercial transport operators carry passengers to and from the station. Businesses emerge around the movement of people. When the train stops, that movement stops with it. The question therefore extends beyond the railway itself: What happens to the people whose livelihoods have become connected to the railway? Reports from the resumption of service at Ujevwu in late 2025 captured renewed calls from stakeholders for the Federal Government to procure more trains, with the argument that rail could reduce pressure on Nigerians travelling by road. That demand points to another contradiction. Nigeria needs more dependable public transportation. Yet the railway that should provide part of that alternative has itself experienced repeated interruptions. Is this abandonment? To say that government has abandoned the Ujevwu–Itakpe corridor would require more evidence than a series of service interruptions. The government and the NRC have continued to repair the line, investigate incidents and announce plans for safer operations. The NRC’s latest report specifically says the corporation is committed to strengthening railway safety, improving operational resilience and restoring public confidence. The unanswered question Perhaps the most revealing thing about Ujevwu is that the railway itself has never disappeared. The tracks are still there. The station is still there. The investment is still there. What keeps disappearing is the certainty that the train will be there when people need it. That is why the story of Ujevwu–Itakpe cannot be reduced to a question of whether government built a railway. It did. The more difficult question is whether government can sustain it. Can the authorities provide reliable services? Can the railway be maintained properly? Can passengers travel without fear? Can vandalism be prevented? Can technical failures be addressed before they become emergencies? Can the people whose lives and businesses depend on the corridor plan their lives around a timetable they can trust? Until those questions are answered consistently, Ujevwu will remain a place of waiting. Waiting for the train. Waiting for reliability. Waiting for safety. The challenge is not merely to bring political leaders into the same room, but to secure an agreement that can withstand the pressures of presidential ambition, party interests and the struggle for control of a joint campaign. From declarations to commitments The Director of Media and Publicity of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Kola Ologbondiyan, told Saturday Vanguard that the opposition still has an opportunity to reach an arrangement before the election. “I strongly believe that the opposition can mount a credible challenge to President Tinubu before the January 2027 election. And my belief is based on the decision reached at the meeting held in Ibadan among all the opposition political parties to look at that proposed grand alliance. The decision reached by the majority of the opposition parties was that, at the nick of time, they were going to pull together,” he said. Ologbondiyan expressed confidence that the parties could still realign, despite the disagreements and political movements that have complicated efforts to build a common platform. His optimism comes amid renewed consultations involving six opposition parties and presidential candidates, including Atiku Abubakar, Obi, Seyi Makinde, Donald Duke and Adewole Adebayo, over a framework for cooperation ahead of the 2027 polls. The consultations followed calls for sustained dialogue and coordinated action among opposition parties. Yet, agreement to continue talking is different from an agreement on who should emerge as the coalition’s presidential candidate. Tinubu may win without unity of opposition —Ben Obi Senator Ben Obi, who told Saturday Vanguard that he had taken it upon himself to facilitate discussions among leading opposition figures, believes the consequences of failure could be significant. “I believe very strongly that if the opposition does not come together, the incumbent might coast to victory. So, I gave myself an assignment,” Senator Obi said. “Seyi Makinde is like my younger brother, just as Peter Obi is. Atiku is my boss and my friend, and we are like one family. So, I approached the three of them and took time to work things out with them. “I said to myself that if the opposition did not come together, we would be wasting our time.” Obi said he initiated discussions among Makinde, Peter Obi and Atiku, asking each of them to nominate two trusted associates to participate in a six-person committee. He subsequently approached former Ekiti State Governor Kayode Fayemi to coordinate the meetings. “I told Kayode Fayemi, ‘Don’t allow the meeting to die,’” Obi said. “They will not agree to step down for anybody. But, from the way I see things, we may reach a stalemate (at the polls in January, 2027). If that happens, this committee could become the answer.” Whether the committee can help resolve that dilemma will depend on its mandate, the willingness of the principals to accept its recommendations and the extent to which any eventual understanding becomes binding. Ambition meets ideology For Comrade Mark Adebayo, Chief Communications Adviser to the Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign, who spoke to Saturday Vanguard, the timing of the negotiations is itself a major obstacle. “I think the biggest obstacle to such a possibility (of a united front) is the time factor,” Adebayo said. “The conversations around different political Parties coming together to support a single presidential ticket came too late in the day, in my opinion. That’s a conversation that should have begun at least three years ago by building critical political infrastructures to achieve that. You can’t start such a crucial process on the eve of a general election.” Opposition woke up late Adebayo argued that a coalition requires more than last-minute consultations, pointing to the need for political structures capable of sustaining joint mobilisation and translating agreements among leaders into coordinated action across the country. He also identified ideological differences among the parties and their presidential candidates as a fundamental obstacle. “Secondly, the differences in political and governance ideologies of the various Parties and candidates would also constitute fundamental obstacles to such possibility,” he said. “I think the opposition woke up to that realization too late. Meanwhile, while I agree it is extremely challenging, it is not impossible for one presidential candidate to defeat the incumbent.” Adebayo said a successful challenge would require extensive mobilisation around a common political programme, adding that Prince Adewole Adebayo was working towards that objective. His position raises a question that extends beyond the timing of the negotiations: how much ideological agreement is necessary for opposition parties to work together? item.title: Moviegoers in frenzy as ‘Issakaba: The Return’ is set for November cinema release
item.description: By Benjamin Njoku Two years after it was shot in early 2024 in Asaba, Delta State, the highly anticipated Nollywood action-thriller “Issakaba: The Return” is finally set for its cinematic release in Nigeria on Friday, November 13, 2026. The director and co-producer, Lancelot Imasuen, disclosed this during a press screening of the sequel last weekend in Lagos. The film sees veteran actor Sam Dede returning as the fearless Ebube. The original “Issakaba” was first released in 2001 and was inspired by real-life vigilante movements. Following the continued relevance of its theme, the decision to revisit the classic was made. Since its trailer dropped online, moviegoers have been eager to storm the cinemas for the much-awaited sequel. And true to expectations, the blockbuster is worth the buzz it is currently generating. The sequel recaptures the evil the Issakaba Boys fought 25 years ago, which is still very much present today, making “Issakaba: The Return” a must-watch. Speaking at the event, Lancelot, fondly called D’Gvnor, recalled how “Issakaba” was born out of real-life events in Aba, following the success of his earlier hit “The Last Burial,” produced by the late Jude Chukwuka Emelionwu of Kas-Vid International. “After “Last Burial” was making waves, my attention was drawn to the activities of the Bakassi Boys in Aba. We called a script conference with Reginald Ebere, started discussing casting and characterisation, and that was how “Issakaba” was born. It was originally titled “My Town,” he disclosed. According to him, the film’s message remains urgent: “Issakaba said security is local. item.title: Oyebanji Pledges To Prioritise Job Creation, Agriculture, Begins Second Term

Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubu congratulated Governor Oyebanji on his inauguration for second term in office, urging him to consolidate on his previous achievements to deliver more dividends for the people of the state. Tinubu, represented by the Vice President, Senator Kashim Shettima at the ceremony in Ado-Ekiti, described Oyebanji’s victory as a testament of the trust that residents have in his administration and by extension, in the All Progressive Congress (APC). He further urged the residents to come en masse on January 16, 2026 and vote for President Tinubu for a second term in office, in order to enjoy more dividends of democracy.
